newsitem.title: USA: COPPER SURPLUS ON HORIZON IN U.S. - DEALERS.
newsitem.headline: COPPER SURPLUS ON HORIZON IN U.S. - DEALERS.

text.p: North American copper producers that were active buyers earlier in the year are expected to move to the sell side of the market, which could speed up the surplus of metal in the U.S. market, dealers said.

Spot merchant premiums are 2.25-2.50 cents over COMEX spot, off from 2.50-3.25 cents two weeks ago and off from recent highs of 4.00-5.00 cents two months ago when Inco Ltd's Sudbury mine was crippled by a month-long strike in June.

At that point, Inco Ltd was buying copper in the spot market to meet its commitments, sources said. But last week, Inco returned to production after a month-long maintenance shutdown in July and is believed to have withdrawn from the spot market.

Noranda Inc has also retreated from the buy side, after aggressively buying in its European commitments early this summer, when its Horne smelter was shut down for maintenance in early June, dealers said.
"There's plenty of copper around," said one brass mill executive. "Inco and Noranda are both shipping often and on time. And I don't believe they need to buy in to meet their obligations."
Kennecott Utah Copper, the Rio Tinto's U.S. subsidiary, is gearing up its 280,000-tonne-per-year Bingham Canyon smelter after two years of production problems.

Traders expect the smelter to be up at full production by the end of the year. And the company has already gone into the market looking for spot customers for September, after spending the better part of the last two years on the buy-side of the market.

"They're a conservative company by nature," said one trader. "They're not going in like gangbusters, certainly not with the problems they've had. But they're poking their head up. And by November, we expect them to be seeking long term contracts with consumers."
"We expect to reach full production sometime in the fourth quarter," a Kennecott executive said, declining to elaborate.

Producers are also finding little solace in the export markets, particularly with stocks in the London Metal Exchange Singapore warehouse having nearly quadrupled in the last eight weeks to 61,850 tonnes.

A recent report by Peter Hollands' Bloomsbury Minerals Economics attributed the warehouse increase to a liquidation of the Chinese strategic reserve, not seasonal demand, an issue that was contested by physical dealers.

"Only about 10,000 tons of the Singapore increase came from China, and it wasn't from the strategic reserve," said one dealer with knowledge of the situation. "About 12,000-14,000 tonnes came from South Korea, either from them directly or from merchants that bought metal from them. And the rest was arbitrage shipments from Shanghai and just weak demand."
"Asia has been very sloppy," said one U.S. exporter. "Business has been very slow, and you can see that by the way that the warehouses have increased here and abroad."

"Business has been good (in the U.S.)," said one merchant. "But the fact remains that a lot of us participated in a lot tenders from Chile thinking that the Chinese were going to come to the party. Guess what? They never came and now we expect that metal to fill the LME warehouses at a rate of 10,000-20,000 tonnes a month through the rest of the year."
LME warehouse stocks totaled 250,400 tonnes in Monday's report, doubling in the last eight weeks to their highest level since September 23, 1996.

On potentially bullish factor is the strike at Falconbridge Ltd's Sudbury complex in Ontario, which is entering its second week. But most physical dealers discounted the strike, noting that the Sudbury produced no refined copper, but instead shipped copper matte to the Timmins refinery in northern Ontario.
"It would take a couple of weeks for the strike to have any impact on the market," said one wire producer."
